name: Ethereum
executive_summary: Ethereum launched in 2015 as a general-purpose smart contract platform, and about a decade later at the time of this scoring it's carrying a privacy application ecosystem worth roughly $4.2 billion in cumulative volume on top of deep institutional and developer adoption, driving a TradFi score of 80. The AI score of 74 is held back mainly by settlement speed: transactions take roughly 13-15 minutes to become fully final, which is slow for an agent trying to act and confirm in real time. The 6-point gap between the two scores comes from that finality lag combined with a fee market that's hard to predict and thin privacy tooling at the base layer.

key_findings: This score covers Ethereum's base layer only, under its current proof-of-stake design -- activity happening on Layer 2 scaling networks that settle back to Ethereum isn't counted in any of these numbers.

Ethereum's three strongest categories -- Developer & Ecosystem, TradFi Approved, and Regulatory & Risk -- all score 90, reflecting genuinely deep penetration on both sides: a large, active base of developers building on the network, and substantial institutional access and regulatory comfort around the asset.

Privacy & Confidentiality lands at a middling 48. Ethereum's base layer has no built-in way to hide a transaction, but a substantial ecosystem of third-party privacy applications has grown on top of it -- roughly $4.2 billion in cumulative volume through tools like Railgun, zkBOB, and Tornado Cash. One related project, Aztec, isn't counted here because it runs its own separate security setup rather than relying on Ethereum's.

Ethereum only partially passes our quantum-computer readiness check, but that check isn't what's holding the score back -- even the strictest ceiling it would impose sits well above where Ethereum actually landed on its category-by-category merits.

Ethereum's transaction-finality speed only earns a partial pass on our AI check, but that check isn't what's setting the score -- Ethereum's category-by-category performance landed just below that check's ceiling on its own.

Execution Layer is a relative weak point at 62, driven mainly by how long it takes for a transaction to become fully and irreversibly final -- roughly 13 to 15 minutes. That's a real constraint for any agent use case where it needs certainty that a payment has settled before it can safely act on it.

Agent Identity & Compliance is Ethereum's strongest category on the AI framework at 83, driven by ERC-8004, an agent-identity standard that originated on Ethereum and has since become widely used across other chains as well.

The 6-point gap between Ethereum's TradFi and AI scores doesn't come from one single weak spot -- it's the combined effect of three separate structural issues: slow final settlement, a fee market where costs can spike unpredictably due to competition for block space, and thin privacy at the base-layer level.

watch_items: An upgrade called Dencun significantly reduced the rate at which transaction fees are permanently removed from circulation ('burned'), which changes Ethereum's supply dynamics. This may justify revising the Tokenomics & Supply score down from 80 toward the 76-78 range at a future reassessment.

Two upcoming upgrades on Ethereum's roadmap, known as Fusaka and Glamsterdam, include changes aimed at making transactions final in a single step rather than over many minutes, along with other performance and storage improvements. If they ship as planned, they could meaningfully raise the Execution Layer score.
